title: Trust but Test
summary: Ferncart stops shipping on hope: build a fast test pyramid, tame flaky tests, and know what tests can never catch.

goals.text: Tell unit, integration, contract and end-to-end tests apart by scope
Shape a test pyramid and know why the cone shape hurts
Keep feedback fast and know which bugs only production reveals

steps.title: Ferncart ships on Thursdays
body: Ferncart delivers groceries in three cities. Fourteen engineers merge code all week, then every Thursday a QA team spends two days clicking through a 90-item checklist before anything reaches shoppers.
It feels safe. In practice, the checklist only covers what somebody remembered to write down, and engineers wait days to learn whether a change broke something.

steps.title: A discount applied twice
body: A tidy-up of the pricing code made promo codes apply once per item as well as once per cart. Carts with two or more promo items got 20% off instead of 10%.
No checklist line covered “two promo items plus a code”, so it sailed through QA. It ran for three days and cost $41,000 before a shopper's tweet flagged it.

callout.text: Manual passes test what people remember. Bugs live in the combinations nobody wrote down.

changes: ~ Cart service now returns wrong totals

steps.title: Unit tests: one piece, in isolation
body: A unit test calls one function or class directly with chosen inputs and asserts on the output. priceFor() needs no server, network or database, so a test runs in milliseconds.
That speed is the point: Ferncart writes 2,400 of them, covering every discount rule and edge case, and they all finish in 18 seconds on a laptop.
The catch: anything the function talks to is replaced by a fake. A fake behaves how you believe the real thing behaves.

steps.title: Integration tests: talk to the real thing
body: All unit tests passed, yet staging lost cents: the database mapping stored amount in an integer column and quietly truncated it. The fake database never would have.
An integration test runs the Cart service against a real Postgres started in a throwaway container, with real migrations and real SQL. It catches wiring, queries and serialization bugs.
Each one takes seconds instead of milliseconds, so Ferncart keeps the count modest: 180 tests, about 3 minutes.
changes: + Postgres runs in a test container

steps.title: Contract tests: pin down the handshake
body: The Payments team renamed a request field to amount_cents. Cart's tests used a stubbed Payments that still accepted the old name, so everything stayed green while real checkouts failed.

A consumer-driven contract fixes this: Cart records exactly what it sends and what it needs back. Payments' CI replays that contract against its real API on every pull request, so a breaking rename fails their build before merge.

callout.text: Contracts replace most cross-team end-to-end tests: each side is tested alone, against a shared, versioned promise.

steps.title: End-to-end: a robot shopper
body: An end-to-end test drives a real browser through the deployed stack: sign in, search, add to cart, pay. It is the only test that proves all the pieces actually fit together.
It is also the slowest and most fragile: every network hop, animation and shared environment is a chance to fail. Ferncart keeps just 12 journeys, the ones that would make the news if they broke.

steps.title: Many small tests, few big ones
body: Stack the layers and you get a test pyramid: a wide base of fast, precise unit tests, fewer integration and contract tests, and a thin tip of end-to-end journeys.

The rule of thumb: catch each bug at the lowest layer that can see it. A discount rule belongs in a unit test; a broken SQL mapping in an integration test; only “do the services connect?” needs end-to-end.
The inverted shape, the ice-cream cone, is mostly manual and browser tests: slow, flaky, and silent about where the bug is.

steps.title: The test that cried wolf
body: One checkout journey fails about one run in fifteen with no code change. Engineers learn to hit rerun until it goes green.
That habit is the real damage: when a genuine failure appears, people shrug “probably flaky”. A flaky test trains the team to ignore red.

Fixes: wait for a condition (button enabled) instead of a fixed sleep, give each test its own data, quarantine a flaky test out of the blocking suite with an owner and a deadline, and track the flake rate like any other metric.

callout.text: A test that fails at random is worse than no test: it costs time and teaches people to distrust the suite.

steps.title: Fast feedback first
body: A suite nobody waits for is a suite nobody runs. Ferncart reorders CI so the cheapest checks run first and fail fast: lint and unit tests report in 90 seconds.
Integration tests are split across four parallel shards. The end-to-end journeys run after merge on main, in parallel, against a staging copy, and block the deploy, not the developer.

steps.title: What tests can't see
body: Tests run your code on your inputs in a clean room. Production is not a clean room: a query that is instant on 1,000 test rows times out on 38 million, a config value differs, the bank's API slows down, traffic triples at 6 pm.
So testing lowers risk before merge; it never removes it. The bugs that escape are caught by monitoring and by releasing gradually, so a bad change touches a few users for a few minutes.

callout.text: Next: Ship It Safely — pipelines, feature flags and canaries that limit the blast radius of what tests miss.

steps.title: Trust, but test
body:
• Unit: one piece, milliseconds, thousands of them.
  • Integration: real database or broker in a container; catches wiring and SQL.
  • Contract: each side verifies a shared promise instead of a shared environment.
  • End-to-end: a handful of critical journeys only.
  • Kill flakiness fast and keep the first signal under a few minutes.
  • Tests cover code, not production: pair them with monitoring and gradual rollout.
